nodes.text: Speech recognition models that hit human parity on one benchmark degrade sharply when applied to other datasets/domains.
Robustness to distribution shift, not benchmark WER alone, determines real-world usefulness of an ASR system.
Unsupervised pre-training (e.g., wav2vec-style encoders) scales to very large unlabeled audio (up to 1,000,000 hours) but yields only an encoder that still needs a fine-tuned decoder/LM per task.
Some prior work instead pools several existing human-labeled datasets (e.g., a 5,140-hour, 7-dataset combination) to improve generality.
Neither approach scales the supervision itself — pairing audio with text targets, however noisy — to the size that unsupervised pre-training already reaches.

Can scaling weakly supervised multitask, multilingual audio-text data by roughly an order of magnitude beyond prior supervised work produce a model that generalizes zero-shot across datasets, languages, and tasks?

Build and evaluate Whisper: one sequence-to-sequence model trained to predict transcript/translation/timestamp text directly from audio, using lightly filtered internet-sourced supervision at 680,000 hours.

Encoder-decoder Transformer family (Tiny to Large, 39M-1550M params), trained multitask (transcription, X-to-English translation, language ID, timestamps) via a single text-based output format, no dataset-specific fine-tuning at evaluation time.

680,000 hours: 438,218 h English ASR, 117,113 h non-English ASR across 96 languages, 125,739 h X-to-English translation; lightweight automated filtering rather than manual QA; 30-second audio segments paired with aligned transcript text; trained ~2-3 epochs (220 updates) with AdamW, no augmentation/regularization.
Controlled dataset-scaling experiment: medium-sized models trained on 0.5%, 1%, 2%, 4%, 8%, 100% of the data (3,405-681,070 hours) with early stopping.
Controlled model-scaling comparison across the five model sizes on the same task suite (recognition, multilingual recognition, translation, language ID).
Zero-shot Whisper Large V2 reaches 2.7% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean, comparable to mid-2019 supervised SOTA.
Despite comparable LibriSpeech performance to supervised models, Whisper reduces error by 55.2% on average relative to a supervised LibriSpeech baseline across 12 other datasets (zero-shot).
Whisper is more robust to additive pub noise below 10 dB SNR than all 14 compared LibriSpeech-trained models.

The gap between matched benchmark performance and out-of-distribution robustness indicates that LibriSpeech-trained models overfit to that dataset's specific acoustic/textual style, while Whisper's broad training data avoids this.
On multilingual recognition (Fleurs), log(WER) correlates with log(training hours per language) at r²=0.83; WER halves for every 16x increase in per-language data.
On X-to-English translation, the analogous correlation is much weaker (r²=0.24) and Whisper still reaches a new zero-shot SOTA of 29.1 BLEU on CoVoST2 X-to-en.
The weaker translation correlation is attributed to noisier training labels for translation (e.g., audio language-ID errors), not to translation being inherently harder to scale.
Whisper underperforms on VoxPopuli (13.6% WER vs 9.1-10.6% for XLS-R/mSLAM) and on Fleurs language ID (64.5% vs 77.7% SOTA on the full 102-language set; 80.3% on the 82 overlapping languages).

Dataset-size scaling: English WER falls from 30.5% (3,405 h) to 9.9% (681,070 h); multilingual WER falls from 92.4% to 29.2%; X-en BLEU rises from 0.2 to 24.8; gains are rapid up to ~13k-54k hours and diminish toward the full dataset.
Model-size scaling: English WER on LibriSpeech test-clean falls from 6.7% (Tiny) to 4.2% (Large V2), with similar monotonic gains on multilingual, translation, and language-ID tasks.
Joint multitask/multilingual training underperforms English-only training at small model/compute scale but overtakes it at the largest scale tested (negative-to-positive transfer crossover).

On 7 long-form datasets, Whisper outperforms the best open-source system (NVIDIA STT); on a 25-recording human-transcribed subset of Kincaid46 it comes within 1.15 WER points of a computer-assisted professional transcription service.

An ablation over long-form decoding heuristics (beam search, temperature fallback, VAD, previous-text conditioning, timestamp constraints) shows each intervention incrementally reduces average WER from 11.0% to 10.0% across the 7 long-form datasets.

Training data is 65% English; most other languages have under 1,000 hours; the Whisper-developed text normalizer risks being overfit to Whisper's own output patterns (checked against an independent normalizer).

It remains unclear whether Whisper's robustness comes from its trained encoder, its trained decoder (acting as an audio-conditioned language model), or both; this is not directly tested. Remaining errors in long-form transcription are increasingly structural (hallucination, repetition) rather than perceptual, and scaling has not clearly fixed them.
Weakly supervised pre-training at scale is a viable, and comparatively underexplored, route to robust, general-purpose speech systems that need no per-dataset fine-tuning.
Authors point to targeted data collection for low-resource languages, and to studying fine-tuning and encoder/decoder ablations, as unstudied next steps.

Scaling weakly supervised multitask, multilingual training data to 680,000 hours produces a single ASR/translation model whose zero-shot generalization across datasets, languages, and noise conditions substantially exceeds same-benchmark-trained supervised systems, following a predictable relationship with data and model scale.
